title: How TanStack Query caches, deduplicates, prefetches, and rolls back
description: Many of the big decisions in a React frontend come down to *where data lives* and *when you fetch it*. This quiz starts with the split between **server state** (a cached copy of data you don't own) and **client state**. Then it covers document vs. normalized caches, request deduplication, optimistic updates and rollback, request waterfalls, prefetching, `staleTime`, and how Suspense changes component design. The examples use React and TanStack Query.

questions.title: What separates server state from client state?
questions.description: Teams often use TanStack Query or SWR for API data, but plain `useState`, Zustand, or Redux for things like whether the sidebar is open.

options.text: Server state is an **asynchronous cache of data someone else owns**, and it can go stale without the client knowing. So it needs caching, staleness rules, background refetching, and deduplication. Client state belongs to the app and changes synchronously, so you only need to store and read it.
Server state is any data stored in a database, and client state is any data held in JavaScript variables.
Server state must be global and client state must be local to a component. The split is only about scope.
Server state is read-only and client state is writable, so they need different tools.

questions.explanation:
The TanStack Query docs and its maintainer TkDodo describe **server state as a cache of data you don't own**. You only hold a copy. The source of truth is a remote server, other clients can change it at any time, and your copy can go stale without you noticing. That one property is why server state needs caching, a freshness policy (`staleTime`), background revalidation, request deduplication, retries, and garbage collection.

Client state, like the theme, which modal is open, or an unsaved form draft, belongs to the app. It changes synchronously and has one source of truth, the app itself. A reducer or `useState` is enough.

The wrong answers focus on side details. Where the bytes live doesn't matter, since you can persist client state to a database and server state sits in memory. Scope is a separate question. Client state is often global (the theme), and server data is often used in a single component. And you can write server state with mutations. You just write through it to a source you don't control.
questions.references: [TanStack Query: Does TanStack Query replace client state?](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/does-this-replace-client-state)

questions.title: Which of these are client state?
questions.description: You're deciding what goes into a server cache library (TanStack Query) and what stays in ordinary client state (`useState` or a store). Select **all** that apply.

options.text: The current UI theme (light / dark).
Whether a confirmation modal is currently open.
The text a user has typed into a search box but not yet submitted.
The list of orders returned by `GET /api/orders`.

questions.explanation:
Ask two questions about each item. Who owns the source of truth, and can it change without you knowing?

- **Theme.** The app owns it, and no server changes it. Client state.
- **Modal open or closed.** Temporary UI. Client state.
- **Unsubmitted search text.** A draft that exists only in the browser until the user submits it. Client state. The results it fetches after submit are server state.
- **`GET /api/orders`.** A copy of data the backend owns, which other clients can change. This is the classic case for a server cache library. Cache it, mark it stale after `staleTime`, dedupe concurrent reads, and refetch in the background.

A common mistake is putting fetched API data in Redux or Zustand and then writing loading flags, refetch logic, and cache invalidation by hand. That rebuilds a query cache from scratch. Keep server state in the cache library and use your store for real client state.

questions.title: Why does the roster still show the old name?
questions.description: You're using TanStack Query with default settings, and two queries hold the same user. The profile screen reads `['user', 7]`. A team roster reads `['team', 'roster']`, and each roster entry includes the user's name. A mutation renames user 7 and writes the new name into `['user', 7]` with `setQueryData`. The profile updates right away, but the roster keeps the **old** name until it refetches.

options.text: TanStack Query is a **document cache keyed by query key**, not a normalized entity cache. Each query keeps its own copy of user 7, so writing to `['user', 7]` doesn't touch the copy inside `['team', 'roster']`. That copy stays old until you invalidate or refetch the roster.
`['team', 'roster']` has a `staleTime` that's too high, so it ignored the update.
React's reconciler skipped the roster because the array reference didn't change.
Apollo Client would behave the same way. No client cache can push an entity update across separate queries.

questions.explanation:
TanStack Query stores each query result as a whole document under its query key. It doesn't split your data into entities, so it can't tell that `['user', 7]` and the user object inside `['team', 'roster']` are the same user. Updating one document leaves the other unchanged.

A **normalized cache**, like Apollo Client's, splits responses into one store keyed by entity identity (for example `User:7`). Every query points at that one record, so a single write shows up everywhere. That's why the Apollo option is wrong. Sharing updates across queries is the main selling point of a normalized cache.

With TanStack Query you keep queries consistent yourself, usually by **invalidating** the other query:

```ts
// after the rename mutation succeeds
queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['team', 'roster'] });
```

`staleTime` has nothing to do with it. It controls when a query refetches, not whether one query's write reaches another. React also re-rendered correctly. The roster simply still holds the old data.

questions.title: How many network requests go out?
questions.description: Three components mount in the **same render**. Each one calls `useQuery({ queryKey: ['user', 7], queryFn: fetchUser })` with default options, and the cache is empty.
questions.explanation:
**One.** TanStack Query deduplicates requests by query key. The first component that needs the data starts a fetch. Any other component that subscribes to the same key while that request is in flight shares the **same promise** instead of starting its own. All three components use one request and one cache entry, and they re-render together when it resolves.

That's why you can call `useQuery` for the same data in many components without coordinating them. The cache does the coordinating. Deduplication has limits, though. Three different keys fire three requests. And once a request resolves, it's no longer in flight, so a later mount may trigger a background refetch if the data is stale (see `staleTime`).

questions.title: Why cancel queries before an optimistic write?
questions.description: The standard optimistic update recipe calls `await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey })` at the top of `onMutate`, *before* it saves a snapshot and writes the optimistic value.

options.text: A background refetch for that key may already be running. If it resolves **after** your optimistic `setQueryData`, it overwrites your value with server data that doesn't include your change yet. Cancelling in-flight fetches prevents that race.
It stops the mutation itself from being sent to the server twice.
It clears the cache entry so your optimistic value starts from scratch.
You need it to get the `context` object that `onError` uses for rollback.

questions.explanation:
An optimistic update races the network. Say a refetch for `['todos']` was already running when the user clicked. You call `setQueryData` with the optimistic value, and a moment later the older refetch resolves and writes its pre-mutation result on top. The user sees their change disappear. `cancelQueries` aborts in-flight fetches for the key, so nothing overwrites your write:

```ts
onMutate: async (newTodo) => {
  await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] }); // stop in-flight refetches
  const previousTodos = queryClient.getQueryData(['todos']); // snapshot for rollback
  queryClient.setQueryData(['todos'], (old) => [...old, newTodo]); // optimistic write
  return { previousTodos }; // becomes `context` in onError / onSettled
}
```

`cancelQueries` doesn't deduplicate the mutation. It doesn't clear the cache either. You *snapshot* the cache so you can roll back. And the rollback `context` is whatever you **return** from `onMutate`, not something `cancelQueries` gives you.

questions.title: Which statements about optimistic updates in `useMutation` are true?

options.text: The value you return from `onMutate` becomes the `context` argument of `onError` and `onSettled`. That's where you keep the snapshot for rollback.
`onError` rolls back by writing the snapshot back into the cache with `setQueryData(queryKey, context.previous)`.
`onSettled` usually calls `invalidateQueries`, so the cache matches the server after the mutation finishes, whether it succeeded or failed.
Optimistic updates need a normalized cache, so they don't work with TanStack Query's document cache.

questions.explanation:
The callbacks work together around the cache:

- **`onMutate(variables)`** runs before the request. It cancels in-flight queries, snapshots the current data, applies the optimistic write, and **returns** the snapshot. TanStack Query passes that return value on as `context`.
- **`onError(err, variables, context)`** runs if the mutation fails. You restore `context.previous` with `setQueryData`, which undoes the optimistic change.
- **`onSettled`** runs after success *or* failure. Invalidating the key triggers a refetch, so the cache ends up matching the server either way.

The false option has it backwards. Optimistic updates are *easiest* with a document cache, because you write the predicted result straight into the query's data. A normalized cache is another valid approach, but you don't need one.

questions.title: What makes this loader slow, and how do you fix it?

options.text: It's an unnecessary **request waterfall**. `fetchConfig` doesn't depend on `user`, but `await` makes it wait until `fetchUser` resolves, so the total is about 400 ms. Start both requests first and `await Promise.all([...])` to run them at the same time (about 200 ms).
Nothing is wrong. Sequential `await`s already run concurrently in JavaScript.
Wrap each call in `useMemo` so the results are cached between renders.
Add a `staleTime` so the second request is served from cache.

questions.title: Which techniques help remove request waterfalls?

options.text: Start independent requests together and `await Promise.all([...])` instead of awaiting them one by one.
Move fetching up to the route or loader so it starts before components render (render-as-you-fetch), instead of having each component fetch after it mounts (fetch-on-render).
Use `useQueries` to run a dynamic list of queries in parallel instead of nesting components that each fetch.
Raise `staleTime`, and TanStack Query will run independent first-load requests in parallel automatically.

questions.explanation:
A waterfall happens when a request can't *start* until an earlier one finishes. Every fix changes when requests start:

- **`Promise.all`** runs requests that don't depend on each other at the same time.
- **Render-as-you-fetch** moves the fetch out of the component tree, into a route loader or an event handler, so it starts right away. With fetch-on-render, the parent renders, the child mounts and fetches, then the grandchild mounts and fetches, and so on.
- **`useQueries`** runs N queries at once from a single hook call, so you don't need a chain of nested components that each fetch.

`staleTime` is the wrong answer. It controls freshness (whether a cached query refetches), not parallelism. On a cold first load nothing is cached, so raising `staleTime` doesn't change how the requests are scheduled.

questions.title: What does `prefetchQuery` on hover do?

options.text: It fetches the post and stores it in the cache before navigation. When the detail page's `useQuery({ queryKey: ['post', id] })` mounts, the data is already there, so the page renders without a loading spinner.
It renders the detail component ahead of time in a hidden offscreen tree, ready to swap in.
It opens a subscription that streams live updates for the post until you navigate away.
It does nothing unless the post is already cached. Prefetching can only refresh existing entries.

questions.explanation:
`prefetchQuery` runs the same fetch `useQuery` would, but you call it yourself, ahead of time. It writes the result into the cache and returns a promise that resolves to nothing, so you don't read its value. The user spends a few hundred milliseconds moving to the link and clicking, and the fetch happens during that time. The next page then renders instantly from the cache.

It doesn't render any component (React does that after navigation), and it doesn't open a stream. It also works on an empty cache, which is the whole point: it fills an entry that doesn't exist yet. Also note that `prefetchQuery` respects `staleTime`. If a fresh copy is already cached, it skips the network, so repeated hovers cost nothing.

questions.title: How do you stop refetching data that never changes?
questions.description: `useQuery({ queryKey: ['currencies'], queryFn: fetchCurrencies })` loads a list of currency codes that **never** change during a session. With default options, the request fires *every time* you navigate back to the page.

options.text: Set a high `staleTime`, for example `staleTime: Infinity`. The query then counts as fresh, and no background refetch runs on mount, window focus, or reconnect.
Increase `gcTime` so the cache entry lasts longer between visits.
Wrap `fetchCurrencies` in `useCallback` so its identity stays stable across renders.
Set `networkMode: 'offlineFirst'` so the network is skipped when data exists.

questions.explanation:
The refetch happens because the **default `staleTime` is `0`**. Data goes stale as soon as it arrives, so every remount, window focus, and reconnect finds a stale query and refetches it in the background. For data that doesn't change during a session, set `staleTime: Infinity`. TanStack Query then serves the cached data and never refetches it automatically.

Why the other options don't work:

- **`gcTime`** sets how long an *inactive* query stays in memory before it's garbage collected. Here the entry was still in the cache. It was *stale*, not removed, so a longer `gcTime` doesn't stop the refetch.
- **`useCallback`** keeps the function reference stable, but the cache ignores it. The query key drives refetching, not the identity of `queryFn`.
- **`networkMode`** controls what happens around connectivity, like pausing while offline. It doesn't decide whether to reuse cached data that's fresh enough.

questions.title: How does `useSuspenseQuery` change your component?
questions.description: You switch a component from `useQuery` to `useSuspenseQuery({ queryKey: ['post', id], queryFn: () => fetchPost(id) })`.

options.text: `data` is always defined inside the component, so there's no `isPending` or `undefined` branch to handle. The nearest `<Suspense>` boundary shows its fallback while the data loads, and an `<ErrorBoundary>` catches fetch errors.
`data` can still be `undefined` on the first render, so you keep the same loading check you had with `useQuery`.
It turns off caching for that query and refetches on every render.
It only works in React Server Components and can't run on the client.

questions.explanation:
With Suspense, loading and error states move out of the component. `useSuspenseQuery` suspends rendering until the data exists, so when your component body runs, `data` is always there. TypeScript types it as `TData`, not `TData | undefined`, and the `if (isPending) return <Spinner/>` checks go away. The loading UI moves up to the nearest `<Suspense fallback={...}>`, and an `<ErrorBoundary>` catches fetch errors:

```tsx
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<Failed />}>
  <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
    <Post id={id} /> {/* uses useSuspenseQuery; renders only with data */}
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>
```

The cache works the same way, with the same query keys, `staleTime`, and deduplication. Only the way you read the data changes. It runs on the client and doesn't need Server Components.

Watch out for two `useSuspenseQuery` calls in the *same* component. They run one after the other, because the first one suspends before the second starts, and that's a waterfall again. Use `useSuspenseQueries` to fetch them in parallel.

questions.title: Which `useMutation` callback runs *before* the mutation function?
questions.description: In this callback you cancel in-flight queries, snapshot the current cache value, apply the optimistic update, and return a context object for rollback.
questions.explanation: It's **`onMutate`**. It runs before `mutationFn` and receives the same `variables` you passed to `mutate(...)`. Whatever it returns comes back to you as `context` in `onError` and `onSettled`, which is how the rollback snapshot is still around if the request fails. The full order is `onMutate`, then `mutationFn`, then `onError` or `onSuccess`, then `onSettled`. The optimistic write and the rollback snapshot both start in `onMutate`, so it's the main step in the optimistic update recipe.
